question:
For Spastic ataxia 11, autosomal dominant (OMIM #621226), caused by variants in TUBA4A: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Clinical phenotypes reported in affected individuals with frequency as numerator and denominator per cohort, original paper wording, and standard HPO term if identifiable, attached to a resolvable source (PMID or DOI)
Most discriminating findings present in most affected individuals but uncommon in differential diagnoses/confused disorders, naming those disorders and stating the confidence of the distinction
Findings looked for and found absent in affected individuals whose presence argues against the diagnosis
Differences in phenotype by variant type, position, age, or sex
Findings that one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts

prior.text: SPAX11 cannot be distinguished with certainty from other autosomal dominant spastic ataxias (such as SPG7-related spastic ataxia, SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, or other SPAX entities) based on clinical phenotype alone. Instead, identification relies on a characteristic core dyad of progressive spastic paraparesis combined with cerebellar ataxia in the absence of severe autonomic failure, severe cognitive impairment, or prominent lower motor neuron signs, followed by definitive molecular testing of TUBA4A.
candidate_answers: Core clinical phenotypes include cerebellar ataxia (gait ataxia, dysmetria, dysarthria; standard HPO: HP:0001251) and lower limb spasticity/pyramidal signs (hyperreflexia, extensor plantar response; HPO: HP:0002061), accompanied by cerebellar atrophy on MRI (HPO: HP:0001272) in approximately 80-100% of affected adults in reported pedigree series.

The most discriminating phenotypic combination against classic hereditary spastic paraplegias (pure HSPs) is the prominent early cerebellar syndrome and cerebellar atrophy on neuroimaging; however, distinguishing SPAX11 from SPG7 or spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA1, SCA2, SCA3) is low-confidence based purely on clinical signs due to nearly identical spastic-ataxic overlap.

Features consistently absent or atypical in SPAX11 that argue strongly against the diagnosis when present early include severe early dementia, prominent optic atrophy or retinopathy (unlike SCA7), and prominent lower motor neuron denervation without ataxia (which would point toward ALS22 or other motor neuron diseases).

Genotype-phenotype divergence occurs based on the specific TUBA4A variant and domain: specific dominant-negative or destabilizing mutations cause classic upper/lower motor neuron disease (ALS22), whereas distinct SPAX11 missense variants selectively impair microtubule dynamics causing spastic ataxia with incomplete penetrance or variable age of onset.

d21.rationale: Benkirane et al. demonstrated altered microtubule dynamics in patient fibroblasts; correlating specific biophysical parameters of tubulin polymerization across different alleles (such as p.Glu415Lys vs de novo variants) could explain differences in cerebellar degenerative penetrance.

d22.question_text: What structural and biophysical properties distinguish TUBA4A variants that cause isolated myopathy (CMYO26) from those causing SPAX11, ALS/FTD, or combined multisystem proteinopathy?
d22.rationale: Understanding how different missense mutations perturb microtubule lattice incorporation, dynamic instability, or kinesin/dynein transport in cerebellar neurons versus sarcomeric structures in myocytes will explain why only specific variants bridge spastic ataxia and myopathy.

d23.question_text: To what extent do patients clinically diagnosed with SPAX11 have subclinical myofibrillar myopathy, neuromuscular junction transmission defects, or elevated serum creatine kinase?
d23.rationale: Systematic neuromuscular assessment (repetitive nerve stimulation, muscle MRI, and CK profiling) in SPAX11 cohorts will determine whether pure spastic ataxia truly lacks muscle involvement or if myopathy is underrecognized.

d24.rationale: Compiling unified individual-level phenotyping tables across both Torella et al. and Benkirane et al. cohorts will refine the statistical confidence intervals for speech versus oculomotor signs in TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia.

d26.rationale: While bedside eye movement evaluation shows overlapping broken pursuit and nystagmus, quantitative oculomotor recordings may uncover distinguishing sub-phenotypic profiles across these spastic ataxia genotypes.

d27.question_text: What is the true penetrance and phenotypic spectrum of non-p.Glu415Lys missense variants in TUBA4A across large international hereditary spastic paraplegia and ataxia cohorts?
d27.rationale: Currently described SPAX11 cohorts primarily center on p.Glu415Lys; systemic multi-cohort screening will establish whether variant type or location influences the prominence of lower limb spasticity versus cerebellar and ocular motor manifestations.

d28.question_text: Does human post-mortem histopathology in SPAX11 patients demonstrate exclusive or primary Purkinje cell loss, or is there concurrent loss of granule neurons and deep cerebellar nuclei neurons?
d28.rationale: While animal models carrying Tuba4a missense mutations exhibit prominent selective Purkinje neuron degeneration, direct validation in post-mortem human cerebellar tissue across different disease durations is required to verify whether Purkinje loss is the sole primary driver of macrostructural cerebellar atrophy.

d29.question_text: Can volumetric 7T MRI of the cerebellar cortex distinguish Purkinje-layer predominant atrophy from granule cell layer atrophy in early-stage TUBA4A mutation carriers?
d29.rationale: Establishing high-resolution imaging biomarkers across early and late disease stages would clarify whether cortical cerebellar volume loss follows a spatiotemporal pattern reflecting initial Purkinje cell loss progressing to vermian and hemispheric atrophy.

d30.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence and longitudinal progression of subclinical vs. clinical axonal neuropathy across all genetically confirmed SPAX11 pedigrees stratified by age decile?
d30.rationale: Currently, detailed nerve conduction studies have only been reported in isolated adult SPAX11 probands. Prospective electrophysiological testing across asymptomatic or younger mutation carriers will delineate whether subclinical axonal loss precedes spastic ataxia.

d31.question_text: Do different TUBA4A mutations (e.g., p.Glu415Lys vs. p.Gln176Pro vs. FTDALS9-associated variants) exhibit differential disruption of microtubule stability and axonal transport in peripheral motor and sensory axons?
d31.rationale: TUBA4A is associated with pure spastic ataxia, myo-tubulinopathy, and ALS/FTD. Comparing axonal transport kinetics in iPSC-derived sensory and motor neurons across variants will clarify the cell-type specific vulnerability.

d32.question_text: What is the exact individual-level breakdown of dysarthria severity, nystagmus type (horizontal, vertical, gaze-evoked, downbeat), and broken smooth pursuit in the supplementary tables of Benkirane et al. (2024)?
d32.rationale: Extracting the raw supplementary clinical tables from Benkirane et al. will allow exact pooled numerator/denominator calculations (e.g., n/24 total published SPAX11 patients) for speech and specific oculomotor sub-phenotypes.

d33.question_text: Do patients with TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia demonstrate vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) abnormalities or saccadic dysmetria, and how do their oculomotor profiles compare directly to FGF14 (SCA27B) and AFG3L2 (SPAX5/SCA28)?
d33.rationale: Both SCA27B and SCA28 present with spasticity and downbeat/gaze-evoked nystagmus. Determining whether TUBA4A exhibits distinct saccadic abnormalities or downbeat nystagmus provides essential clinical bedside discriminator metrics.

d34.question_text: What are the exact patient-by-patient disease durations and corresponding standardized MRI cerebellar atrophy scores (vermis vs hemispheres) for each of the 12 patients in the Benkirane et al. (2024) cohort compared to the Torella et al. (2023) p.Glu415Lys pedigree?
d34.rationale: Directly testing individual-level duration-versus-score data from the supplementary clinical tables of both primary discovery papers will decisively prove or refute whether the atrophy discrepancy is explained by scan timing or variant locus.

d35.question_text: Do longitudinal repeat MRI scans in individual TUBA4A SPAX11 patients demonstrate quantifiable progressive cerebellar atrophy over a 3-to-5 year follow-up window?
d35.rationale: Longitudinal intra-individual imaging trajectories provide the most rigorous proof that normal initial imaging in early-stage SPAX11 evolves into the severe pancerebellar atrophy reported in advanced cases.

d36.question_text: What is the exact frequency and breakdown of cerebellar dysarthria versus specific oculomotor signs across all non-p.Glu415Lys TUBA4A missense variants in the Benkirane et al. cohort?
d36.rationale: While Torella et al. report 100% nystagmus and infrequent dysarthria for p.Glu415Lys, examining whether allele-specific differences exist across other TUBA4A variants is needed to solidify the penetrance threshold.

d37.question_text: Can quantitative video-oculography differentiate TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia from other early-stage autosomal dominant spastic ataxias such as SPAX/HSP phenocopies?
d37.rationale: Since ocular signs like nystagmus and broken pursuit occur early and with high penetrance, objective oculometric biomarkers could serve as a sensitive clinical discriminator.

d38.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Differences in semi-quantitative cerebellar atrophy scores across TUBA4A SPAX11 patients are driven primarily by variant-specific biochemical disruption of microtubule polymerization rather than disease duration alone, such that de novo catalytic-core missense variants cause accelerated pancerebellar atrophy within fewer than 5 years of onset while C-terminal inherited variants (e.g., p.Glu415Lys) progress indolently.

d39.rationale: Directly testing volumetric loss per year across genotype groups will settle whether variant location independently determines neurodegenerative tempo or if indolent atrophy is an artifact of ascertainment.

d40.question_text: How do tubulin polymerization dynamics and MAP/motor protein interaction kinetics differ biochemically between p.Glu415Lys and central globular core variants in vitro?
d40.rationale: Measuring in vitro microtubule catastrophe, polymerization rates, and kinesin motility will elucidate whether C-terminal modifications selectively preserve polymerization while altering transport.

d41.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): The severity score of cerebellar atrophy on brain MRI in TUBA4A SPAX11 exhibits a positive correlation with disease duration from symptom onset, such that patients imaged within 5 years of symptom onset reliably demonstrate absent or minimal cerebellar volume loss, whereas moderate-to-severe pancerebellar atrophy only develops after at least 10 to 15 years of active clinical disease.
d41.rationale: deep test refuted it: The literature does not support the hypothesis that cerebellar atrophy severity correlates predictably with disease duration, nor that patients imaged within 5 years reliably show absent or minimal atrophy while moderate-to-severe atrophy only appears after 10 to 15 years. Current human clinical reports (Torella et al., 2023; Benkirane et al., 2024; OMIM #621226) document variable presence of cerebellar atrophy (e.g., detected in 7 of 11 cases in Benkirane et al., and absent or slight in several patients in Torella et al.), but do not establish a duration-dependent linear correlation or temporal cutoffs of 5 versus 10-15 years.

d42.question_text: Does quantitative volumetric MRI of the cerebellum correlate longitudinally with disease duration in prospective TUBA4A SPAX11 cohorts?
d42.rationale: Current evidence relies on semi-quantitative or qualitative descriptions (atrophy present in 7/11, or slight/absent). Formal voxel-based morphometry is required to test true duration-dependent atrophy kinetics.

d43.question_text: Do specific TUBA4A variant alleles (e.g., p.Glu415Lys vs de novo missense alleles) dictate the presence and severity of cerebellar atrophy independently of disease duration?
d43.rationale: Different variants may exhibit distinct pathogenic effects on microtubule stability and dynamics, which could explain the variability in cerebellar atrophy across kindreds.

d44.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): The emergence of cerebellar dysarthria in TUBA4A spastic ataxia (SPAX11) correlates strictly with advanced disease duration (>10 years from motor onset) rather than being an early presenting phenotype.
d44.rationale: deep test refuted it: The literature does not substantiate a strict correlation between the appearance of cerebellar dysarthria and a disease duration of >10 years in TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia (SPAX11). In the primary describing study (Torella et al., 2023), dysarthria is described inconsistently across affected individuals and is not universally present even in long-standing disease, nor is there systematic prospective or cross-sectional natural history data establishing a 10-year threshold before bulbar/speech manifestations can emerge.

d45.question_text: What is the systematic cross-sectional frequency and onset timing of speech/bulbar involvement across all known TUBA4A mutation carriers?
d45.rationale: Standardized longitudinal speech assessments and SARA speech subscores across multi-center cohorts are necessary to define whether dysarthria onset correlates with duration, variant locus, or overall disease severity.

d46.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): De novo TUBA4A missense variants reported in Benkirane et al. produce a significantly higher incidence of early-onset dysarthria than the familial inherited p.Glu415Lys variant reported by Torella et al.
d46.rationale: deep test refuted it: The literature does not support the hypothesis that de novo TUBA4A missense variants produce a significantly higher incidence of early-onset dysarthria compared to the familial p.Glu415Lys variant. Both Benkirane et al. (2024) and Torella et al. (2023) identify spastic ataxia, lower limb hyperreflexia, and cerebellar signs such as dysarthria as shared core features across both inherited and de novo cases without demonstrating any statistically significant divergence in dysarthria onset or prevalence. Furthermore, OMIM #621226 lists dysarthria as a common finding across SPAX11 cases in general, and no data establish preferential early-onset speech involvement in de novo cases.

d47.question_text: Do de novo TUBA4A missense mutations cause significantly more severe microtubule polymer incorporation defects in vitro compared to the inherited p.Glu415Lys variant?
d47.rationale: Direct biophysical comparison of tubulin dimer incorporation and dynamic instability between de novo variants and inherited mutations can objectively evaluate whether de novo variants exert stronger dominant-negative effects.

d48.question_text: What is the systematic age at onset of dysarthria and gait ataxia in a combined multicenter registry of all molecularly confirmed SPAX11 cases?
d48.rationale: Systematic collection of standardized HPO phenotypic terms across all known carriers will determine whether subtle genotype-phenotype correlations exist regarding bulbar involvement.

d49.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): Cerebellar volume loss in SPAX11 follows a stereotyped anatomical sequence where vermian volume loss precedes cerebellar hemispheric atrophy by at least five years of symptom duration, rendering isolated vermian atrophy the earliest objective MRI sign of SPAX11.
d49.rationale: deep test refuted it: There is no longitudinal or quantitative neuroimaging evidence supporting a stereotyped anatomical sequence in SPAX11 where vermian atrophy precedes hemispheric atrophy by at least five years. In the definitive clinical report describing SPAX11 (OMIM #621226) caused by the TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys variant (Torella et al., 2023), brain MRI demonstrated only 'slight or absent cerebellar atrophy' and 'questionable upper vermis atrophy'. No systematic five-year latency between vermian and hemispheric loss has ever been observed or documented.

d50.question_text: What are the quantitative volumetric MRI trajectories of the cerebellar vermis versus hemispheres in longitudinal follow-ups of TUBA4A mutation carriers?
d50.rationale: SPAX11 has only recently been defined in two kindreds; serial volumetric 3D T1 MRI data are required to establish whether true cerebellar volume loss occurs and whether it follows a regional gradient.

d51.question_text: Does neurofilament light chain (NfL) elevation precede or correlate with detectable neuroimaging changes in presymptomatic or early symptomatic TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys carriers?
d51.rationale: Establishing fluid biomarker timelines will resolve whether axonal damage occurs well before subtle vermian or cerebellar changes can be reliably identified on neuroimaging.

h5.text: Cerebellar atrophy penetrance on MRI in TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia (SPAX11) is duration- and variant-dependent rather than an obligate feature (80-100%), showing normal cerebellar volume early in disease course or in milder alleles such as p.Glu415Lys.
h5.rationale: Resolves the direct contradiction between Benkirane et al. (2024), who report penetrant cerebellar atrophy in hereditary spastic ataxia probands, and Torella et al. (2023), who identified normal brain MRIs in affected individuals with shorter disease duration or specific alleles.
h5.screen_note: Literature confirms variation in cerebellar atrophy on MRI ranging from severe atrophy in some TUBA4A cohorts to slight or absent atrophy in patients with p.Glu415Lys.

h6.text: Specific TUBA4A missense mutations cause a continuous spectrum bridging pure spastic ataxia (SPAX11) and myo-tubulinopathies, where cerebellar atrophy occurs concomitantly with progressive myofibrillar or skeletal myopathy.
h6.rationale: Clarifies whether TUBA4A-associated cerebellar atrophy is confined to pure spastic ataxia or extends into neuromuscular presentations, which would alter differential diagnosis against pure cerebellar ataxias and HSPs.
h6.screen_note: Recent literature identifies overlapping TUBA4A phenotypes where ataxia and skeletal myopathy co-occur, including mouse models and human cohorts presenting with multisystem proteinopathy.

h7.text: Purkinje neuron loss is the primary histological driver of cerebellar volume loss in TUBA4A-induced spastic ataxia, causing progressive vermian and hemispheric atrophy that increases with clinical disease duration.
h7.rationale: Explains why younger or recently affected patients may have normal or borderline cerebellar volumes on MRI whereas older individuals with long-standing disease exhibit pronounced cerebellar atrophy.
h7.screen_note: A mouse model of TUBA4A spastic ataxia (SPAX11) exhibits overt ataxia and Purkinje neuron degeneration, supporting Purkinje cell loss as a primary driver of cerebellar pathology.

h8.text: In the index SPAX11 kindreds carrying TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys (12 affected individuals across two families), dysarthria is present in only an intermediate subset (<50%) of affected individuals, whereas oculomotor abnormalities (nystagmus and broken smooth pursuit) show higher penetrance (>70%) among clinically evaluated patients.
h8.rationale: Discovery descriptions of the TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys cohort explicitly qualify dysarthria as appearing 'sometimes', while highlighting oculomotor signs such as nystagmus and broken smooth pursuit alongside gait and spasticity. Defining exact cohort frequencies establishes whether speech impairment is an obligate or dispensable diagnostic criterion for SPAX11.
h8.screen_note: The original study describing 12 SPAX11 patients with TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys across two families notes oculomotor signs and specifies that dysarthria occurred only 'sometimes'.

h9.text: Peripheral neuropathy in SPAX11 is an axonal sensory-motor neuropathy that manifests in adult life rather than early childhood, occurring in a minority of affected individuals with TUBA4A variants.
h9.rationale: In the discovery report, peripheral nerve conduction studies performed at age 40 revealed an axonal sensory-motor neuropathy with electromyographic signs of denervation. Determining whether this feature is universal across adult family members or restricted to later-stage/older individuals will clarify whether normal nerve conduction studies exclude SPAX11.
h9.screen_note: SPAX11 caused by TUBA4A variants causes progressive spastic ataxia with variable age of onset and reported adult-onset peripheral neuropathy, making the hypothesis biologically and clinically plausible.

h10.text: The combination of broken smooth pursuit and nystagmus with lower limb spasticity differentiates SPAX11 from pure hereditary spastic paraplegias (such as SPG4), but fails to reliably distinguish it from AFG3L2-related spastic ataxia (SPAX5/SCA28) and TUBB4A-related disorders without genetic confirmation.
h10.rationale: Both AFG3L2-associated disorders (SCA28/SPAX5) and TUBB4A-related disorders frequently present with cerebellar eye movement disorders (nystagmus, broken pursuit), dysarthria, and spasticity, mimicking the TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys clinical picture.
h10.screen_note: SPAX11 (TUBA4A) presents with spastic ataxia and oculomotor signs (nystagmus, broken pursuit), differentiating it from pure HSP but overlapping clinically with other spastic ataxias and tubulinopathies.

h11.text: Across all published TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia kindreds (Torella et al. and Benkirane et al.), oculomotor signs (nystagmus and broken smooth pursuit) show near-complete penetrance (>85% of clinically evaluated cases), whereas cerebellar dysarthria is present in fewer than 50% of affected patients.
h11.rationale: In the index p.Glu415Lys kindreds (Torella et al.), nystagmus is documented in all 12 evaluated affected individuals (12/12) and broken smooth pursuit is nearly universal, while dysarthria is explicitly qualified as only occurring 'sometimes'. Testing whether this discrepancy holds when pooling with the multicentric cohort of Benkirane et al. (12 additional patients across diverse missense alleles) establishes whether oculomotor signs are primary diagnostic red flags compared to bulbar/speech involvement.
h11.screen_note: The literature confirms that SPAX11 was defined by Torella et al. (2023) and expanded by Benkirane et al. (2024), making an evaluation of oculomotor versus dysarthric phenotypic penetrance across these cohorts coherent and testable.

h12.text: The emergence of cerebellar dysarthria in TUBA4A spastic ataxia (SPAX11) correlates strictly with advanced disease duration (>10 years from motor onset) rather than being an early presenting phenotype.
h12.rationale: If oculomotor signs like gaze-evoked nystagmus and broken pursuit occur at symptom onset but speech remains normal until late in the disease, clinicians can exclude early-onset spastic ataxias characterized by early, severe bulbar involvement (such as ARSACS or certain SCA subtypes) when evaluating early spastic-ataxic patients.
conflicts: No prospective or natural history study demonstrates that dysarthria emerges strictly after 10 years of disease duration in SPAX11; dysarthria expression is variable rather than strictly time-dependent.
h12.screen_note: TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia (SPAX11) presents primarily with gait disturbances and early oculomotor signs, making a late onset of cerebellar dysarthria plausible.
h12.bin_reason: refuted: The literature does not substantiate a strict correlation between the appearance of cerebellar dysarthria and a disease duration of >10 years in TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia (SPAX11). In the primary describing study (Torella et al., 2023), dysarthria is described inconsistently across affected individuals and is not universally present even in long-standing disease, nor is there systematic prospective or cross-sectional natural history data establishing a 10-year threshold before bulbar/speech manifestations can emerge.

h13.text: De novo TUBA4A missense variants reported in Benkirane et al. produce a significantly higher incidence of early-onset dysarthria than the familial inherited p.Glu415Lys variant reported by Torella et al.
h13.rationale: De novo mutations in tubulin genes typically exert stronger dominant-negative effects on microtubule lattice integration than mildly deleterious inherited variants. Comparing patient-level data between de novo cases and multi-generational familial cases will reveal whether speech motor pathways are preferentially vulnerable in de novo tubulinopathies.
h13.screen_note: Both cohorts (Benkirane et al. de novo cases and Torella et al. p.Glu415Lys families) report spastic ataxia with dysarthria, providing a concrete basis to compare phenotypic severity and onset across inheritance modes.
h13.bin_reason: refuted: The literature does not support the hypothesis that de novo TUBA4A missense variants produce a significantly higher incidence of early-onset dysarthria compared to the familial p.Glu415Lys variant. Both Benkirane et al. (2024) and Torella et al. (2023) identify spastic ataxia, lower limb hyperreflexia, and cerebellar signs such as dysarthria as shared core features across both inherited and de novo cases without demonstrating any statistically significant divergence in dysarthria onset or prevalence. Furthermore, OMIM #621226 lists dysarthria as a common finding across SPAX11 cases in general, and no data establish preferential early-onset speech involvement in de novo cases.

h14.text: The severity score of cerebellar atrophy on brain MRI in TUBA4A SPAX11 exhibits a positive correlation with disease duration from symptom onset, such that patients imaged within 5 years of symptom onset reliably demonstrate absent or minimal cerebellar volume loss, whereas moderate-to-severe pancerebellar atrophy only develops after at least 10 to 15 years of active clinical disease.
h14.rationale: Resolving whether semi-quantitative MRI cerebellar atrophy scores correlate linearly with time from symptom onset directly reconciles the apparent phenotypic discrepancy between cohorts reporting moderate-to-severe atrophy (Benkirane et al., 2024) and kindreds reporting normal cerebellar imaging early in the disease course (such as early p.Glu415Lys carriers). If proven true, a normal cerebellar MRI cannot rule out early-stage SPAX11.
h14.screen_note: Cerebellar atrophy is variable in TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia (SPAX11), ranging from normal/slight to overt atrophy across cohorts, making a duration-dependent progression model clinically and biologically plausible.
h14.bin_reason: refuted: The literature does not support the hypothesis that cerebellar atrophy severity correlates predictably with disease duration, nor that patients imaged within 5 years reliably show absent or minimal atrophy while moderate-to-severe atrophy only appears after 10 to 15 years. Current human clinical reports (Torella et al., 2023; Benkirane et al., 2024; OMIM #621226) document variable presence of cerebellar atrophy (e.g., detected in 7 of 11 cases in Benkirane et al., and absent or slight in several patients in Torella et al.), but do not establish a duration-dependent linear correlation or temporal cutoffs of 5 versus 10-15 years.

h15.text: Differences in semi-quantitative cerebellar atrophy scores across TUBA4A SPAX11 patients are driven primarily by variant-specific biochemical disruption of microtubule polymerization rather than disease duration alone, such that de novo catalytic-core missense variants cause accelerated pancerebellar atrophy within fewer than 5 years of onset while C-terminal inherited variants (e.g., p.Glu415Lys) progress indolently.
h15.rationale: If duration from symptom onset is matched between de novo and inherited SPAX11 kindreds but severe cerebellar atrophy remains restricted to de novo or specific mutational domains, the discrepancy between reported cohorts cannot be dismissed as a simple imaging timeline artifact. Testing this distinguishes an intrinsic genotype-structural mechanism from uniform temporal neurodegeneration.
conflicts: The hypothesis asserts that all de novo catalytic-core variants trigger rapid pancerebellar atrophy within <5 years, whereas Johari et al. identified de novo core mutations associated with only mild cerebellar atrophy or predominant skeletal myo-tubulinopathy.

No prospective or retrospective cohort has formally applied standardized semi-quantitative cerebellar atrophy scales matched directly by disease duration between C-terminal (p.Glu415Lys) and catalytic-core cohorts.

Variable penetrance and broad ranges of onset age in both inherited and de novo TUBA4A cases indicate that disease duration and genetic background contribute alongside intrinsic biophysical disruption.

h16.text: Cerebellar volume loss in SPAX11 follows a stereotyped anatomical sequence where vermian volume loss precedes cerebellar hemispheric atrophy by at least five years of symptom duration, rendering isolated vermian atrophy the earliest objective MRI sign of SPAX11.
h16.rationale: Determining the spatial sequence of volume loss will clarify whether discordant MRI findings across studies reflect differential regional sensitivity (isolated vermian vs diffuse hemispheric) rather than a binary present/absent atrophy distinction, providing an early imaging diagnostic marker.
conflicts: The hypothesis asserts a proven 5-year chronological progression from vermian to hemispheric atrophy, whereas clinical reports describe imaging findings merely as 'slight or absent cerebellar atrophy' with 'questionable upper vermis atrophy'.
h16.screen_note: Reports of SPAX11 (TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys) note early or isolated upper vermian cerebellar changes on brain MRI, making the hypothesized temporal sequence biologically plausible for further testing.
h16.bin_reason: refuted: There is no longitudinal or quantitative neuroimaging evidence supporting a stereotyped anatomical sequence in SPAX11 where vermian atrophy precedes hemispheric atrophy by at least five years. In the definitive clinical report describing SPAX11 (OMIM #621226) caused by the TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys variant (Torella et al., 2023), brain MRI demonstrated only 'slight or absent cerebellar atrophy' and 'questionable upper vermis atrophy'. No systematic five-year latency between vermian and hemispheric loss has ever been observed or documented.
